title_en: Fragments from Book Two Against Theodore of Mopsuestia
author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: Cyril writes against Theodore of Mopsuestia's teaching that the Lord was a mere inspired man, defending the unity of God the Word and the flesh assumed for our salvation.
argument: Cyril argues that Christ is one and the same both God and man, not a mere inspired human being. He insists that the divine Word, who existed before the ages unmixed with body and bodily things, assumed flesh for our salvation, remaining impassible in divinity while passible in flesh. Because the life-giving Word made the death-bound flesh his own, he overcame death and corruption in it and transmits that grace to us. As we fell into death in Adam, so in Christ we are refashioned toward incorruption.

outline.move: Cyril cites Christ's command not to call anyone teacher on earth, arguing that when Christ gave this command he was not separating his own divinity from his visible body.

Cyril warns against accepting the Lord as a mindless man, as Theodore's party says, and confesses one and the same Christ as God before the ages unmixed with body and as man assumed for salvation, so that the whole fallen human being might be refashioned.
Cyril explains that because the life-giving Word, who is life by nature, became flesh, human nature blossomed into life, and he became first in all things.
Cyril concludes that the life-giving Word made death-bound flesh his own to overcome death and corruption and transmit incorruption to us, as in Adam we fell into death.

scripture: Cyril cites the Gospel of Matthew in Greek; the saying about the one teacher uses καθηγητής (leader/guide), corresponding to Matthew 23:8 or 23:10. He also cites Colossians 1:18 for 'first in all things'.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; the 430s is approximate.
The addressee is not stated in the surviving fragments.
The precise extent of the original work is unknown.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν καθηγητής, ὁ Χριστός
_unresolved_facts.fix: The form in the source is καθηγητής (lowercase, not capitalized as a title/name form); it appears as a common noun in the quotation, not as a source form for Christ. The actual forms are Χριστός, Χριστῷ, Χριστοῦ, Κύριος, Κύριον, δοῦλος, δοῦλος ὁρώμενος, Σωτῆρος, Σωτῆρος.
The actual form in the source is Σωτῆρος (genitive), not Σωτήρ (nominative).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Quoted saying introduced by 'he said to the disciples'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The introduction is 'ΤΟΙΣ μαθηταῖς ἔλεγε' ('To the disciples he was saying/used to say'), not simply 'he said to the disciples'—the imperfect ἔλεγε indicates ongoing/repeated speech, not a single quotation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Theodore's party (paraphrased opponents) introduced by 'ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι' ('as they themselves say'), referring to those who accept the Lord as a mindless man
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μηδὲ ἀπατάσθωσαν ἄνθρωπον ἄνουν δεχόμενοι τὸν κυριακὸν, ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν καὶ Θεόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The phrase 'ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι' refers specifically to their terminology 'τὸν κυριακὸν' ('the Lordly one'/'the one of the Lord'), not to accepting the Lord as a mindless man. The structure is: 'let them not be deceived accepting the Lordly one, as they themselves say [it], rather [let them accept] our Lord and God.' The 'mindless man' (ἄνουν) is Cyril's characterization of what they do, not what they say.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He insists that the divine Word... assumed flesh for our salvation, remaining impassible in divinity while passible in flesh
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: παθητὸν σαρκὶ, ἀπαθῆ θεότητι, περιγραπτὸν σώματι, ἀπερίγραπτον θεότητι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses datives (σαρκὶ, θεότητι, σώματι, θεότητι) meaning 'passible in respect of flesh, impassible in respect of divinity,' not 'while passible in flesh' which suggests temporal simultaneity. The Greek expresses the mode or respect, not a temporal state.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyril cites Christ's command not to call anyone teacher on earth
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Μὴ καλέσητε διδάσκαλον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation uses διδάσκαλον (teacher), but Cyril's commentary immediately uses καθηγητής (leader/guide) as the key term: 'εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν καθηγητής, ὁ Χριστός.' The brief should note that Cyril shifts from διδάσκαλον to καθηγητής in his exposition.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyril warns against accepting the Lord as a mindless man, as Theodore's party says
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μηδὲ ἀπατάσθωσαν ἄνθρωπον ἄνουν δεχόμενοι τὸν κυριακὸν, ὡς αὐτοὶ λέγουσι, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν καὶ Θεόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyril warns against accepting 'a mindless man' (not 'the Lord as a mindless man'); the 'as they themselves say' modifies 'τὸν κυριακὸν' not the 'mindless man' characterization. The structure is: 'let them not be deceived accepting a mindless man [as] the Lordly one, as they say [it], rather [accepting] our Lord and God.'
